results.summary: This project implements three current-switching digital-to-analog converters (DACs) intended for generating analog VGA display signals. Each DAC uses a 16x16 matrix of unit current sources to convert 8-bit digital inputs into analog current sinks, and a digital controller generates VGA timing and test patterns. The design requires external pull-up resistors and op-amp circuits to convert the current outputs to voltage levels suitable for a VGA display. The documentation is incomplete, with testing procedures and external hardware details marked as 'TBC', but the design is notable for its transistor-level analog implementation and use of OpenLane 2 for the digital controller.

This design is a 60 Hz RMS pump-out controller ASIC that manages a liquid pump by measuring current via a current transformer to detect when a tank is empty. It includes an ADC interface, status LEDs, a relay output, and buttons for manual control and configuration. The chip is intended for industrial pump control and has been tested using FPGA emulation and a custom development board. The documentation is thorough, covering RTL simulation, gate-level testing, and FPGA prototyping, but the design is complex and requires external hardware such as an ADC, current transformer, and relay.

This project implements a USB CDC to UART bridge, allowing a USB host to communicate with a UART device at a fixed 115200 baud rate. It is based on the tinyfpga_bx_usbserial design and requires external USB breakout hardware and a 1.5k ohm pull-up resistor. Silicon test reports confirm that the device enumerates correctly and performs loopback and external UART communication without errors. The design is notable for its successful silicon validation and straightforward implementation.

This is a UART template design created in Wokwi, intended to be connected to an Arduino for testing. It provides a 7-segment display output and minimal documentation, with no detailed explanation of its functionality. The design appears to be an educational template for UART communication, but the documentation is too thin to determine its exact behavior or capabilities.

This design implements a customizable digital padlock that uses switches to set a code and a push button to enter it. A 7-segment display shows 'L' for locked and 'U' for unlocked based on the entered code. The design is created in Wokwi and requires no external hardware, making it suitable for educational purposes. The documentation provides clear instructions for setting and testing the code.

This project is an 8-bit reverse counter with reset, implemented using a series of D flip-flops. It outputs the count on 8 pins, which can be connected to LEDs for visual feedback. The design is created in Wokwi and includes reset and step buttons for testing. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand its function.

This project implements a 32-bit Fibonacci linear feedback shift register (LFSR) with taps at registers 32, 30, 26, and 25, designed to generate pseudo-random sequences. It includes initialization logic to prevent an all-zero state and provides 8 outputs from the rightmost registers. The design is created in Wokwi and can be tested using a logic analyzer, with a provided expected output sequence. Silicon test reports confirm that it generates random-looking output and can be manually initialized.

This design is a 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product using full adders. It is implemented in Verilog and has no external hardware requirements. The documentation is very brief, stating only that it was tested using idle cases, and provides no further details on testing or usage.

This project is a 3-bit 8-channel PWM driver that generates PWM signals on 8 output pins, with each channel's duty cycle set by a 3-bit register. It uses a 3-bit counter and allows setting the PWM level for each channel via input pins. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires no external hardware beyond the clock and control signals. The documentation explains the functionality and testing procedure clearly.

This design provides a P latch and an N latch to verify that $_DLATCH_N_ can be properly techmapped and hardened. It includes inputs for enable and data signals and outputs for the latched values. Silicon test reports confirm that both latches function as expected, with the P latch transparent when enable is high and the N latch transparent when enable is low. The design is a simple test case for standard cell mapping.
